Executive summary

Recommended path: Port to .NET 10 incrementally (strangler fig): new ASP.NET Core host with YARP in front, System.Web adapters for shared code, CoreWCF for the inventory service, EF 6.5 as a bridge before EF Core.

Nothing blocks the move for good: the 4 hard blockers (HttpContext.Current in a library, BinaryFormatter, the WCF server, System.Web in a library) all have known fixes. The risk is behavior, not code - 9 pricing and cart quirks that customers see. Lock them with parity tests before touching anything, then move the read-only pages and the API first.

Top risks

  • high Pricing and cart quirks change silently (order total ignores coupon/VAT, ViewState price, 3-for-2 per line, rounding)
  • high Sign-in breaks while two apps run (Forms auth ticket + machineKey)
  • medium Session cart lost between old and new pages
  • medium API clients depend on 302 redirects from [Authorize] endpoints
  • medium Deleting a product deletes its order history (EF6 cascade)

How the move works: strangler fig

Nothing is rewritten in one go. A new .NET 10 app sits in front of the old one. Every request it can already handle stays in the new app; everything else falls through to the old app. One route at a time moves over - after parity tests prove the new route answers like the old one.

  end
  subgraph oldapp["Old app (.NET Framework)"]
    legacy["LegacyShop.Web<br/><small>everything not migrated yet</small>"]
  end
  yarp -- yes --> done
  yarp -- no / fallback --> legacy
  done -. "remote session + remote auth<br/>(System.Web adapters)" .-> legacy

Risks and how to reduce them

ImpactRiskMitigation
highPricing and cart quirks change silently (order total ignores coupon/VAT, ViewState price, 3-for-2 per line, rounding)Parity tests on the cart and checkout flow + characterization tests on PriceCalculator before any change. Decide quirk by quirk: keep or fix on purpose.
highSign-in breaks while two apps run (Forms auth ticket + machineKey)Remote authentication through the System.Web adapters until the login page moves; then switch to ASP.NET Core cookie auth in one release.
mediumSession cart lost between old and new pagesRemote session (System.Web adapters) while both apps run; move cart pages together; serialize CartLine as JSON.
mediumAPI clients depend on 302 redirects from [Authorize] endpointsCheck API consumers. .NET 10 returns 401 - document it as a breaking change or keep the redirect on purpose.
mediumDeleting a product deletes its order history (EF6 cascade)Decide Restrict vs Cascade in the EF Core model; add a soft delete if history must stay.
lowProduct images use System.Drawing (Windows-only on .NET 6+)Stay on Windows hosting at first, or move to ImageSharp/SkiaSharp (check the licenses).

Questions for the team

  • Do any API consumers rely on the XML format or on the 302 redirect from /api/orders/mine?
  • Which pricing quirks are bugs you want fixed, and which are business rules?
  • Where will .NET 10 run - IIS on the same Windows server, or containers?
  • Does anything outside this solution call the WCF inventory service?
  • Can the BinaryFormatter cache in App_Data/cache simply be deleted on deploy?

Next steps

  1. Decide the 4 open questions above (1 meeting).
  2. Run migration-safety-net: record parity tests for all 6 pages and 5 API actions, characterization tests for PriceCalculator.
  3. Convert all projects to SDK-style + PackageReference (legacy-package-migrator), multi-target LegacyShop.Core and LegacyShop.Data.
  4. Run yarp-strangler-setup: .NET 10 host in front, everything proxied, remote auth + remote session on.
  5. Move the first slices: Web API (GET endpoints), the image handler, the MVC report, Default.aspx - then Product, Cart, Login, Admin.

How these numbers were made

  • Hours are for one developer who knows the codebase, at 6 focused hours a day.
  • "With AI" = an agent does its share of the work and a developer reviews it (25% of the agent's share goes back into review).
  • Decisions (auth, session, hosting, UI targets) take the same time with or without AI.
  • Fixed costs (hosting, auth, session, config, rollout) are scaled by solution size: x0.5 under 3k LOC, x1 up to 30k, x1.5 above.
  • Ranges, not promises: re-estimate after the first 3 migrated slices.
  • AI share per kind of work: decisions 0%, mechanical changes 90%, translating code 70%, tests and proof 80%, hosting and rollout 30%.
  • Counts (pages, controllers, operations, blockers) come from a deterministic scan of the source. Targets, risks and the verdict were reviewed by an AI agent and should be confirmed by the team.
